newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain unlikely to bend on wage freeze plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain unlikely to bend on wage freeze plan.

text.p: Spain's conservative government, determined to prepare for European monetary union, will not back down on its planned public sector wages freeze despite a threat of a general strike on Wednesday, analysts said on Monday.
"There's too much at stake for the government to back down now," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.

"If the unions were to soften they would lose their last bastion of influence, while the government has no alternative to a wage freeze to meet its (monetary union ) budget criteria for 1997," he added.

Unions called a strike for December 11 as part of their battle with the government over its plans to freeze public sector wages in 1997. They have rejected a last-ditch attempt by the government majority Popular Party to avert the strike with a promise to raise salaries in 1998 and 1999 to compensate for the freeze.
Analysts said the government was unlikely to relent, because it claims the wage freeze is vital to bring its finances in line in the run-up to European Monetary Union (EMU), due in 1999.
It could, however, consider adjusting the finer points of its offer, they added.

"The government will probably opt for the minimum policy by playing tough on the wage freeze but eventually giving in to some form of compensation," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.

Urrutia said cracks were already starting to appear in the government's stance with Catalan leader Jordi Pujol, a member of the governing coalition, saying he would offer Catalonia's civil servants compensation for the freeze.
Another issue is that is that the seven-month-old government wants to set an example, some analysts said.
"The government is using the civil servants as a showcase for all other wage negotiations," said Urrutia.
Aside from its wage freeze, the government is also pressing unions and employers for extensive labour market reform.
Analysts said the fact that the government was tackling the unions on two separate issues at the same time made an early agreement unlikely.
Reform talks are due to begin in the first few weeks of 1997, but the government has threatened to legislate if an agreement is not reached or if the pact is not radical enough.
The government announced in July, shortly after taking power, it would freeze public sector salaries in 1997, sparking a number of demonstrations.

The unions, led by the Workers' Commission (CCOO) and the General Workers' Union (UGT), say the freeze violates a deal with the previous socialist administration which guaranteed wages would rise in line with inflation in 1997.
They said government workers had lost 11.2 percent of their buying power since 1993, saving the government 785 billion pesetas ($6 billion) in the process.
Public sector pay was frozen in 1993 and increased a mere one percent in 1994. It moved up in line with inflation in 1995 and 1996.

The government estimates the freeze will slash 200 billion pesetas off the budget deficit, helping to reduce it to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from a forecast 4.4 percent in 1996. ($1=130.6 Peseta)
